opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, this is one of the parts I find most exciting, because the hard problem is rarely the reasoning itself. It's whether the formal policy actually captures what the customer meant. When you translate a natural-language policy, say an HR document about leave eligibility or an access-control policy, into logic, you get a Boolean structure: conditions, conjunctions, disjunctions, implications. That structure is a gift, because it tells you exactly where the interesting decisions are.

So rather than asking a customer, "Is this formula correct?", which no one outside a logic department can answer, we use the structure to generate concrete scenarios. We can ask the solver for a satisfying assignment, an example situation where the policy says "yes," and then perturb it. Flip one variable and see if the outcome changes. If it does, that variable matters at that point, and we can turn it into a question in plain language: "Suppose an employee has worked here for eleven months instead of twelve, but everything else is the same. Should they still be eligible?" The customer can answer that instantly. They're the domain expert.

You can be quite systematic about it. You look for boundary cases, for places where two rules overlap and might conflict, for variables that never seem to affect the outcome, which often signals that something was mistranslated or left out, and for cases where the policy is silent. Coverage ideas from testing and model checking carry over nicely. You want enough questions that each meaningful branch of the logic gets exercised, but not so many that you exhaust the person.

What's nice is that the answers feed back in. If the customer says, "No, that should be denied," you now have a counterexample, and either the formalization or the original document was wrong. Often it's the document. People discover their policy was ambiguous all along. So the Boolean structure becomes a way of having a structured conversation with the customer, and that's how you build real confidence that the formal artifact means what they think it means, before you start using it to check things like LLM outputs.

r001.rationale: It proposes using solver-generated satisfying assignments as concrete customer scenarios and exercising each meaningful branch of the Boolean logic with questions.

r002.rationale: It recommends exercising meaningful branches without asking too many questions, but does not clearly distinguish representative logical-corner coverage from checking every neighboring assignment.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I find really fun, because it's where the formal methods machinery actually touches a human being. When you write an IAM policy, what you've really written is a Boolean formula over a bunch of variables, right? Principal, action, resource, conditions, all of that. And the policy language has this structure of allow statements and deny statements, with deny taking precedence, so under the hood it's a disjunction of the allows, conjoined with the negation of the disjunction of the denies. Once you see it that way, you can hand it to a SAT solver or an SMT solver, and the solver can answer questions about it.

Now the trick is, the customer didn't write the policy as a logical formula. They wrote it with some intent in their head, and the gap between the intent and what the formula actually says is where all the trouble lives. So the question is, how do you surface that gap? And the answer we landed on is, you use the structure of the formula itself to generate the questions.

Here's what I mean. Take a policy and ask the solver: is there an assignment to these variables such that this policy grants access? If yes, give me a concrete witness. Now you have an example, a principal doing an action on a resource, and you can show it to the customer and say, "Did you mean for this to be allowed?" That's a yes-or-no question a person can answer, even if they couldn't tell you the semantics of a condition key off the top of their head. And you can go the other way too: find something that's denied and ask, "Did you mean for this to be blocked?"

But a random witness isn't very useful. If you just ask the solver for a satisfying assignment you'll get something weird, some action nobody cares about from some region nobody uses. So you lean on the Boolean structure to pick good ones. Every disjunct in the policy, every allow statement, is a reason access could be granted, so you can generate at least one witness per statement and ask about each. Every conjunct in a condition block is a constraint, so you can ask what happens right at the boundary of it, flip one condition at a time and see if the answer changes. If you've got a statement that's subsumed by another, meaning there's no assignment where it matters, that's a question in itself: "This statement never does anything, is that what you intended?" And the comparison case is huge. If the customer changes the policy, you compute the difference between the old formula and the new one, and the solver hands you exactly the accesses that were newly granted or newly revoked. Those are the questions you ask, because those are the places where their intent and the text are most likely to have drifted.

What I like about this is it flips the usual relationship. Instead of the tool saying "trust me, I proved it's fine," which nobody believes, the tool says "here are the specific cases that follow from what you wrote, tell me if they match what you meant." The customer stays the authority on intent. The solver just makes sure no corner of the formula gets to hide.

r001.rationale: It proposes generating concrete solver witnesses from each allow statement and using them to ask customers whether the access should be allowed, with related examples for denials and condition boundaries.

r002.rationale: It describes witnesses per allow statement and flipping conditions one at a time, but does not clearly distinguish representative logical-corner coverage from checking every neighboring assignment.

astra-6.text:
Well, you can think of a policy as a Boolean formula: under these conditions, allow access; otherwise, deny it. And that structure gives you a way to generate very specific questions for the customer. If this condition is true but that condition is false, should access still be allowed?

Rather than asking someone to read a complicated policy and say, “Does this look right?”, you give them concrete cases that distinguish different interpretations of their intent. For example, should someone in this role be allowed to access the resource when they’re outside the specified network? That question tests whether the role and network requirements really need to hold together.

The important thing is that the policy itself can’t tell you what the customer intended. But its Boolean structure can help you find the questions where their answers are most useful, and then check whether the policy agrees with those answers.

r001.rationale: It suggests concrete Boolean-condition cases as questions, but does not clearly propose selecting satisfying assignments from distinct regions of the policy’s Boolean structure.

r002.rationale: It does not distinguish testing representative logical corners from checking every neighboring assignment.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, you can think of a policy as a Boolean formula, and then use that structure to work out which questions are actually useful to ask. If I just generate a lot of examples, many of them may exercise essentially the same part of the policy. What I want are examples that help you distinguish between different possible intentions.

So suppose access depends on a couple of conditions. We can look for a case where changing one condition changes the decision, and ask, “Should this request be allowed?” Then we can change another condition and ask again. That helps the customer see which parts of the policy are doing the work.

The important distinction is that the policy tells us what it does; it doesn’t tell us whether that’s what you wanted. These questions give the customer a way to express that intent through concrete cases, without having to reason about the whole Boolean expression at once.

r001.rationale: It proposes asking about cases where changing conditions changes the decision, but does not clearly say to select satisfying assignments from distinct regions of the Boolean structure.

r002.rationale: It does not distinguish covering representative logical corners from checking every neighboring assignment.
